passage.sceneTitle: The First Morning at the New House
passage.preamble: Roberta, Peter and Phyllis have just moved with their mother from a comfortable town house to an old cottage in the country. They arrived late at night, tired and hungry, and there are no servants to help any more.

numberedLines.text: Next morning Roberta woke Phyllis by pulling her hair gently, but quite enough for her
purpose.
“Wassermarrer?” asked Phyllis, still almost wholly asleep.
“Wake up! wake up!” said Roberta. “We're in the new house--don't you remember? No
servants or anything. Let's get up and begin to be useful. We'll just creep down mouse-
quietly, and have everything beautiful before Mother gets up. I've woke Peter. He'll be
dressed as soon as we are.”
So they dressed quietly and quickly. Of course, there was no water in their room, so
when they got down they washed as much as they thought was necessary under the spout of
the pump in the yard. One pumped and the other washed. It was splashy but interesting.
“It's much more fun than basin washing,” said Roberta. “How sparkly the weeds are
between the stones, and the moss on the roof--oh, and the flowers!”
The roof of the back kitchen sloped down quite low. It was made of thatch and it had
moss on it, and house-leeks and stonecrop and wallflowers, and even a clump of purple
flag-flowers, at the far corner.
“This is far, far, far and away prettier than Edgecombe Villa,” said Phyllis. “I wonder
what the garden's like.”
“We mustn't think of the garden yet,” said Roberta, with earnest energy. “Let's go in
and begin to work.”
They lighted the fire and put the kettle on, and they arranged the crockery for
breakfast; they could not find all the right things, but a glass ash-tray made an
excellent salt-cellar, and a newish baking-tin seemed as if it would do to put bread on,
if they had any.
When there seemed to be nothing more that they could do, they went out again into the
fresh bright morning.
“We'll go into the garden now,” said Peter. But somehow they couldn't find the garden.
They went round the house and round the house. The yard occupied the back, and across it
were stables and outbuildings. On the other three sides the house stood simply in a
field, without a yard of garden to divide it from the short smooth turf. And yet they
had certainly seen the garden wall the night before.
It was a hilly country. Down below they could see the line of the railway, and the black
yawning mouth of a tunnel. The station was out of sight. There was a great bridge with
tall arches running across one end of the valley.
“Never mind the garden,” said Peter; “let's go down and look at the railway. There might
be trains passing.”
“We can see them from here,” said Roberta, slowly; “let's sit down a bit.”
So they all sat down on a great flat grey stone that had pushed itself up out of the
grass; it was one of many that lay about on the hillside, and when Mother came out to
look for them at eight o'clock, she found them deeply asleep in a contented, sun-warmed
bunch.
They had made an excellent fire, and had set the kettle on it at about half-past five.
So that by eight the fire had been out for some time, the water had all boiled away, and
the bottom was burned out of the kettle. Also they had not thought of washing the
crockery before they set the table.
“But it doesn't matter--the cups and saucers, I mean,” said Mother. “Because I've found
another room--I'd quite forgotten there was one. And it's magic! And I've boiled the
water for tea in a saucepan.”
The forgotten room opened out of the kitchen. In the agitation and half darkness the
night before its door had been mistaken for a cupboard's. It was a little square room,
and on its table, all nicely set out, was a joint of cold roast beef, with bread,
butter, cheese, and a pie.
“Pie for breakfast!” cried Peter; “how perfectly ripping!”
“It isn't pigeon-pie,” said Mother; “it's only apple. Well, this is the supper we ought
to have had last night. And there was a note from Mrs. Viney. Her son-in-law has broken
his arm, and she had to get home early. She's coming this morning at ten.”
That was a wonderful breakfast. It is unusual to begin the day with cold apple pie, but
the children all said they would rather have it than meat.
“You see it's more like dinner than breakfast to us,” said Peter, passing his plate for
more, “because we were up so early.”
The day passed in helping Mother to unpack and arrange things. Six small legs quite
ached with running about while their owners carried clothes and crockery and all sorts
of things to their proper places. It was not till quite late in the afternoon that
Mother said:--
“There! That'll do for to-day. I'll lie down for an hour, so as to be as fresh as a lark
by supper-time.”
Then they all looked at each other. Each of the three expressive countenances expressed
the same thought. That thought was double, and consisted, like the bits of information
in the Child's Guide to Knowledge, of a question and an answer.
Q. Where shall we go?
A. To the railway.
So to the railway they went, and as soon as they started for the railway they saw where
the garden had hidden itself. It was right behind the stables, and it had a high wall
all round.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 3. How does Roberta wake Phyllis?

rows.key: By pulling her hair, gently but hard enough.

options.value: By pulling her hair, gently but hard enough.
By shouting at her to wake up.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Roberta does shout, at line 4, and that is after Phyllis has begun to stir. In the window, line 1 answers the stem: 'Next morning Roberta woke Phyllis by pulling her hair'.

options.value: By pulling the blankets off her bed.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A common way to wake someone, and nowhere in this passage.

options.value: Phyllis wakes Roberta by pulling her hair.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who is doing it and who it is being done to.
options.execution: Line 1 runs the other way round: Roberta is the one who acts.

rows.hintCore: Find the sentence that says how, not the one that says what happened next.
rows.walkScript: Start at line 1 and read the whole sentence. It names who wakes whom, and how. The hair-pulling is gentle, but enough to work. Line 4 comes later, once Phyllis stirs.

stem.text: Read lines 4 to 7. Why does Roberta want them up now?

rows.key: So the house is beautiful before Mother gets up.

options.value: So the servants have less to do this morning.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Lines 4 and 5 say there are no servants at all, and this reads as if there are.

options.value: So the house is beautiful before Mother gets up.
So Peter will be dressed as soon as they are.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses lines 6 and 7 word for word; a step in the plan, not the reason for it.

options.value: Because Mother has asked them to help her.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: The whole plan is Roberta's own, made while Mother is still upstairs.

rows.hintCore: Ask what she wants to be true before Mother comes down.
rows.walkScript: Read line 4 to line 7 as one speech. Roberta gives a plan and a reason. The reason is what she wants Mother to find. Everything else is how the plan works.

stem.text: Read lines 8 to 10. Which of these is true about the girls' washing?

rows.key: One of them works the pump while the other washes.

options.value: They wash in their own bedroom.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 8 says there was no water in their room, and this option loses that.

options.value: They wash in a basin.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Basin washing is real in the passage, but at line 11, as the thing compared. In the window, line 9 answers the stem: 'when they got down they washed as much as'.

options.value: One of them works the pump while the other washes.
The splashing spoiled it for them.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Line 10 says splashy but interesting, and this reads the but as a therefore.

rows.hintCore: Read the small joining words. One of them turns the sentence round.
rows.walkScript: Go to line 9 and find the word under. It tells you what they stand beneath. Line 10 then splits the job between them. It also says how they found it: splashy, and interesting all the same.

stem.text: Read lines 16 to 19. What does Roberta's reply show about her?

rows.key: She puts the work first and keeps the garden for later.

options.value: She wants to see the garden before starting work.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 18 turns the garden down for now, and this option loses that turning down.

options.value: She is annoyed with Phyllis for talking about the garden.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Line 18 gives earnest energy, which is eagerness rather than annoyance.

options.value: She thinks the garden will turn out to be a disappointment.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: The passage gives her no opinion of the garden, only the word yet.

options.value: She puts the work first and keeps the garden for later.

rows.hintCore: One small word turns a refusal into a delay. Find it.
rows.walkScript: Read line 18 slowly, and hold on to the word yet. Yet means later, not never. So the garden is delayed rather than dismissed. Line 19 says what comes first instead.

stem.text: Read lines 20 to 23. What do the children use for the table?

rows.key: A glass ash-tray for salt, and a baking-tin for bread.

options.value: A glass ash-tray for salt, and a baking-tin for bread.
A baking-tin for salt, and a glass ash-tray for bread.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Both objects sit in lines 21 and 22, with their jobs the other way round.

options.value: They find all the right things and lay them out.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 21 says they could not find all the right things, and this option drops that.

options.value: Bread and butter, set out ready on the table.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: That table is at line 51, in the forgotten room, and line 23 says they had no bread.

rows.hintCore: Two ordinary objects, two new jobs. Check which goes with which.
rows.walkScript: Start at line 21 and find the two things they borrow. One holds the salt, the other holds the bread. Read which object does which job. Line 23 adds a joke about the bread.

stem.text: Read lines 37 to 43. Why is the bottom burned out of the kettle?

rows.key: They fell asleep outside, so nobody took it off the fire.

options.value: Mother let the fire go out while they slept.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Mother only arrives at line 38, and the fire was out well before she came.

options.value: They fell asleep outside, so nobody took it off the fire.
They built the fire far too big for the kettle.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 42 says the fire had been out for some time, so it was not too fierce.

options.value: They set the kettle on after Mother came to look for them.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Line 41 puts the kettle on at half-past five, hours before the eight of line 39.

rows.hintCore: Put the two clock times side by side, then ask who is indoors.
rows.walkScript: Look at line 41 first, and note the time given there. Line 39 gives a second time, three hours later. In between, the children are asleep on the hillside. Nobody is in the kitchen at all.

stem.text: Look at lines 48 and 49. What does 'agitation' on line 48 mean there?

rows.key: being worried and in a hurry

options.value: the stirring or shaking of a liquid
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: A real sense of the word, and nothing in this room is being stirred.

options.value: the half darkness of the house that night
options.tagChildHint: This word is joined to another one. Work out which of the two the question is asking about before you answer.
options.execution: Line 48 lists darkness beside this word, so the two are separate causes.

options.value: being worried and in a hurry
the excitement of finding a forgotten room
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: That happens at line 46, the morning after, and this word is about the night before. In the window, line 48 answers the stem: 'The forgotten room opened out of the kitchen. In'.

rows.hintCore: The sentence gives two causes. One is the light; this is the other.
rows.walkScript: Read line 48 and line 49 together as one sentence. Something made a door look like a cupboard door. Two causes are given: the light, and this word. This word names how the family felt.

stem.text: Look at lines 50 to 52. Peter says 'ripping' on line 52. What does he mean by it?

options.value: that the pie is wonderful
that the pie is torn into pieces
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: The everyday sense of the word, and line 50 has the pie whole and set out.

options.value: that the table has been beautifully laid
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 52 names what Peter is exclaiming about: pie, at breakfast.

rows.hintCore: Listen to how he says it, not to what the word looks like.
rows.walkScript: Read line 52 and see what Peter is exclaiming about: pie, at breakfast. He cries it out, so the word carries his delight. It praises the pie itself, and not the table it stands on.

stem.text: Read lines 53 to 55. Why did Mrs Viney have to go home early?

rows.key: Her son-in-law had broken his arm.

options.value: She had broken her own arm.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Line 54 names her son-in-law as the one with the broken arm.

options.value: Nobody had told her the family was arriving.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 53 has the supper already laid, so she knew, and line 54 gives her reason.

options.value: Because she had to be back at the house by ten.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Line 55's ten o'clock is her return, which comes after the leaving it is offered for.

options.value: Her son-in-law had broken his arm.

rows.hintCore: The note names a person and an injury. Check which person.
rows.walkScript: Go to line 54 and find the note from Mrs Viney. It gives one reason, about a person in her family. Read who the broken arm belongs to. Line 55 then says when she returns.

stem.text: Read lines 64 to 70. What do these lines show about the three children?

rows.key: All three reached the same idea without saying anything.

options.value: They wrote the question and the answer in a book.
options.tagChildHint: Figures of speech are not facts. Ask what the words are really saying.
options.execution: Lines 67 and 68 say the thought was LIKE a school book, so nothing was written.

options.value: All three reached the same idea without saying anything.
They had agreed on the plan earlier in the day.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 66 has the thought arriving as they look at each other, not before.

options.value: Mother suggested that they go down to the railway.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Line 64 has Mother speaking only about lying down; the thought at line 66 is theirs.

rows.hintCore: Notice what has not happened by the time all three agree.
rows.walkScript: Look at line 66 and see what happens first: they look at each other. Line 67 says all three faces held the same thought. Nobody has spoken yet. Lines 69 and 70 then give that thought.

stem.text: Read lines 26 to 30, then lines 71 to 73. Why could the morning search never find the garden?

rows.key: They searched round the house, but the garden lay behind the stables.

options.value: The house stood in a field, and no garden lay near it.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: Line 29 says no strip of garden touched the house, and line 72 finds the garden.

options.value: They had seen no wall at all, but only imagined it in the dark.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 30 says they had certainly seen it, so the passage rules this out.

options.value: They searched round the house, but the garden lay behind the stables.
The garden had hidden itself away, and the high wall kept it out of sight.
options.tagChildHint: Figures of speech are not facts. Ask what the words are really saying.
options.execution: Line 72's hidden itself is a way of speaking, not something the garden did.

rows.hintCore: Put their way of looking next to the place it turned out to be.
rows.walkScript: Read line 27 and note how they searched: round the house. Now read line 72 and see where the garden actually was. The stables sit across the yard, away from the house. Going round the house could not reach it.

stem.text: The writer keeps making one choice about the order she tells things in. Which is it?

rows.key: We are shown the scene, but told the reason for it only afterwards.

options.value: She shows them creeping down to be useful, and then Mother wakes.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses lines 5 and 6 word for word, and names no choice about order at all.

options.value: She lets Mother explain the whole of it, though the children had missed it.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Mother explains the room, but the kettle and the garden are explained by the narrator.

options.value: We are told what the children do, but never what they feel.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: Line 11 gives Roberta's fun, line 39 their contentment, line 56 a wonderful breakfast.

options.value: We are shown the scene, but told the reason for it only afterwards.

rows.hintCore: Ask when each puzzle is explained, and what we had already seen.
rows.walkScript: Take three puzzles from the story: the kettle, the door, the garden. For each one, find where the passage explains it. The explaining always comes after we have watched the scene. That is the choice she keeps making.
